food.text: The goods exchanged along the trans-Saharan trade routes varied depending on the era. In the 10th century, the Muslim scholar Mutahhar ibn Tahir al-Maqdisi described trade between the Islamic world and sub-Saharan Africa as food and clothing moving south, while slaves, gold, and coconuts moved north in return.

Between 1506 and 1510 CE, the traveler Leo Africanus visited Gao and described it as very civilized compared to Timbuktu. He reported that bread and meat were abundant in the town, though wine and fruit could not be found there.

By the 12th century, the Ghana Empire was master of a trade network through the Senegal river valley that had first been set up by the kingdom of Takrur in the 10th century. This network carried salt from Awlil across the region.

Djenné-Djeno, an ancient trading town in Mali's Niger River Valley, is linked by archaeologists to the domestication of native African rice. By about 800 CE, the city and its surroundings may have held between 10,000 and 27,000 people.

Leo Africanus's early sixteenth-century account of Gao also praised its plentiful melons, cucumbers, and excellent squash. He noted enormous quantities of rice and many sweet water wells. He also described a square where, on market days, huge numbers of slaves, both male and female, were sold. A young girl of fifteen was worth about six ducats, a young man almost as much, and small children about half as much as grown slaves.

art.text: West Africa produced several distinct artistic traditions in the centuries around this era. They include the Bura of Niger (3rd to 10th century CE), the Koma of Ghana (7th to 15th century CE) and the Igbo-Ukwu of Nigeria (9th to 10th century CE).
Around the 10th century, more complex methods of making art developed in sub-Saharan Africa. One of the most notable advances was the bronze work of Igbo Ukwu in what is now Nigeria.

Gao, on the bend of the Niger River, was not only a trading town but also a major manufacturing center. Its craftspeople fashioned carnelian into beads, which were greatly valued in the Sudan and the West African rainforest.

Excluding ancient Egyptian figurative art, Nok sculptures are regarded as the earliest large figurative art in continental Africa. Later West African traditions, including Bura, Koma and Igbo-Ukwu, may have been shaped by the Nok clay terracotta tradition.
Archaeological digs have determined that Gao Ancien was the political center of early Gao. It contained the oldest royal palace discovered in the region.

Bronze and brass castings, often ornamented with ivory and precious stones, became highly prestigious in much of West Africa. Their making was sometimes limited to court artisans, and they were identified with royalty.

Imported pottery and glass recovered from the archaeological site of Gao-Saney suggest it was occupied between the 8th and 12th centuries. The site lies about 4 kilometres east of Old Gao on the eastern bank of the Niger.
Copper ornaments have been found in early Phase III deposits at Djenné-Djeno. Their presence shows that trade networks between West and North Africa date earlier than previously thought.

Archaeological excavations at nearby Igbo-Ukwu, led by Thurstan Shaw, uncovered sophisticated cast copper-alloy vessels and ornaments from a wealthy, specialized society flourishing there by at least the late ninth century. Some finds resemble later Nri ritual objects, but scholars have not confirmed the site was the Eze Nri's capital or royal burial ground.

war.text: In 990, the Ghana Empire conquered Awdaghust and installed its own governor there. The source says this was presumably done for commercial and economic reasons.
In 962, the town of Aoudaghost conquered Awgham with an army of 100,000 camel cavalry. Over 20 kings of the Sudan are said to have paid Awdaghost tribute.

The kings of Gao belonged to the Qanda dynasty and used the title Za. They were likely based downstream in Kukiya before moving to Gao by the early 10th century. Their power was based in cavalry and camelry.

By around the year 1000, the army of the Kanem–Bornu Empire had grown into a powerful force. It was strong enough to control the trade routes near the imperial core. Troops were raised through the chima fief system.
A Soninke clan under Mamadu Sumaare, originally from Wagadu, conquered Takrur in the 9th or 10th century. They established the Manna dynasty and gradually melded into the local culture.

Under their king Tinbarutan ibn Usfayshar, the Sanhaja Lamtuna erected or captured the citadel of Awdaghust, a critical stop on the trans-Saharan trade route. After the Sanhaja union collapsed, Awdaghust passed to the Ghana Empire.

The Sanhaja nomads of the Sahara, converted to Islam in the 9th century, were united in the 10th century. With the zeal of new converts, they launched several campaigns against the "Sudanese", the pagan peoples of sub-Saharan Africa.

Kanem–Bornu's military campaigns beyond its own territory were mostly about raiding and setting up tributary relationships rather than outright conquest. This held for most of the empire's history. The early empire grew wealthy and powerful through the raiding of its neighbors and the export of slaves in exchange for horses. Under Dunama II Dibalemi, wars against the Sao were justified in the name of a jihad, and captives were sold as slaves in exchange for further horses from North Africa.

Around 1035, the Lamtuna chieftain Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn Tifat, also called Tarsina, tried to reunite the Sanhaja desert tribes after their union collapsed. His reign lasted less than three years.

literature.text: Much of what is known about early Gao comes from Arab geographers living in Morocco, Egypt and Andalusia, most of whom never visited the region. They called the town Kawkaw or Kuku. The earliest mention of Gao is by al-Khwārizmī, who wrote in the first half of the 9th century.

Historians are unsure when Ghana's ruling dynasty began. The first identifiable mention of it in written records was made by Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī in 830. Later accounts by Cordoban scholar al-Bakri added further detail in the 11th century.

Arab writers were describing Ghana in the 8th century. Muḥammad ibn Ibrāhīm al-Fazārī listed it as equal in size to the Idrisid state of Morocco and called it the "Land of Gold." In 833 it was featured on al-Khwārizmī's world map.

The term Bilād al-Sūdān, literally "land of the Blacks," was used in Arabic from the earliest Arabic sources, dating from no later than the ninth century CE, and was associated with the export of slaves to the Arab world. Early evidence ties this human trafficking to the Kanem–Bornu Empire around Lake Chad rather than to Gao or Ghana. Michael Gomez argues that the rise of trans-Saharan trade linked the Sūdān ever more closely with slaves.

Al-Ya'qubi described Ghana's king as very powerful and wrote of its gold mines and the number of vassals under him. Al-Masudi, writing in the first half of the 10th century, called the King of Ghana supreme and stressed the kingdom's importance because of its gold trade.

science.text: By 833 CE, the West African Ghana Empire appeared on a world map made by the scholar Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi. Arab writers had already begun describing Ghana as a wealthy state by the 8th century, decades before this map was made.

At Igbo-Ukwu in south-eastern Nigeria, archaeologists uncovered elaborate copper and copper-alloy objects. They also found more than 150,000 glass and stone beads, with much of this activity dated to between the ninth and twelfth centuries CE.

Lead-isotope and trace-element studies of the Igbo-Ukwu metalwork show that most of its copper and lead came from ore sources in the Abakaliki area of south-eastern Nigeria. This supports local or regional production rather than import from Europe or the Mediterranean.

Igbo-Ukwu's metalworking documents technical specialisation and complex craft production in the West African forest zone. This activity predates the better-known copper-alloy traditions of Ife and Benin.

Archaeological evidence from Koro Toro suggests that the region surrounding Kanem saw a considerable development of iron production between about 500 and 1000. These were the formative centuries of Kanem.

politics.text: The Kanem Empire rose in the 8th century in the region to the north and east of Lake Chad. It was known as the Kanem Empire from the 9th century onward, and its successor state Bornu lasted as an independent kingdom until 1900.

In the early medieval Sahel, the Ghana Empire was already known to Arab writers as a wealthy state. Al-Fazārī listed it as equal in size to the Idrisid state of Morocco and called it the "Land of Gold."

The Kingdom of Nri, in what is now southeastern Nigeria, was unusual in the history of world government. Its leader exercised no military power over his subjects. Instead it was a sphere of religious and political influence over a third of Igboland.

The Gao kings belonged to a dynasty called the Qanda and used the title Za. Their power rested on cavalry and camelry. They were probably based downstream in Kukiya before moving to Gao by the early 10th century.

The historian Michael Gomez argues in African Dominion that Gao was West Africa's first city-state. He says it provided the model for the Ghana Empire. This challenges the older story of three successive empires: Ghana, Mali and Songhay.

Early Arab writers described the king of Ghana as a very powerful ruler. Al-Ya'qubi mentions the gold mines and the number of vassals under his authority. Al-Masudi, writing in the first half of the 10th century, calls the king supreme, with vassals beneath him.

The first identifiable written mention of Ghana's imperial dynasty came from al-Khwārizmī in 830. In 833 Ghana was featured on his world map. Historians remain uncertain about when the ruling dynasty actually began.
By the 10th century, the Songhai chiefs had established Gao as a small kingdom. They took control of the people living along the trade routes, laying the foundation for a later empire.

The history of the Kanem Empire is mainly known from the Royal Chronicle, or Girgam. The German traveler Heinrich Barth discovered this chronicle in 1851, long after the empire rose in the 8th century.
Around 990, presumably for commercial and economic reasons, the Ghana Empire conquered Awdaghust. It installed its own governor there, turning a former partner into a directly ruled town.
The Kingdom of Nri was administered by a priest-king called an Eze Nri. He managed trade and diplomacy on behalf of the Nri people and held divine authority in religious matters.

A direct trade route to Egypt was closed during the reign of Ahmad ibn Tulun (868 to 884) because of safety concerns. Ibn Hawqal wrote that some caravans were attacked by bandits and others were overwhelmed by wind-blown sand. Traffic shifted to a route through Sijilmasa.

Writing in the 970s, Ibn Hawqal proclaimed the king of Ghana the wealthiest king on the face of the earth. He also noted that the king maintained relations with the king of Awdaghust, the town Ghana would later conquer in 990.

Around 977, Ibn Hawqal wrote that the king of Awdaghust kept relations with the ruler of Ghana. This suggests Aoudaghost was not yet part of the Ghana Empire. Ghana's kings, he said, badly needed the Awdaghust king's goodwill because of the salt that reached them from the lands of Islam.

Takrur's founding dynasty were said to be blacksmith-kings who introduced iron-working and ore extraction to the region. They were eventually overthrown by the Tonjon dynasty sometime during the 8th century.

Gao was one of the earliest sites of significant trans-Saharan trade, already active in the 8th century, much earlier than scholars used to believe. Gold, copper, slaves and salt were its most important trade items, alongside its carnelian bead making.

Ghana had developed a trade route leading directly to Egypt, used by Egyptian and Nubian merchants to visit the Sudan. It was closed during the reign of Ahmad ibn Tulun, who ruled from 868 to 884, because of safety concerns.

philosophy.text: Nri tradition traces the origin of its sacred kingship to a culture hero named Eri and his son Nri, an ancestry linked to a ruling dynasty that oral king lists place beginning around the tenth century. This origin story framed the Eze Nri's religious authority as inherited directly from that founding ancestor rather than from conquest.

The Kingdom of Nri, centered on Agukwu-Nri in what is now southeastern Nigeria, had no standing army or central administration. Instead its ruler, the Eze Nri, was a sacred king whose authority rested on religion, title-taking, and purification rites, with oral king lists placing the dynasty's beginnings around the tenth century.

In the ninth century, the Arab geographer al-Yaʿqūbī wrote about Gao, an early trans-Saharan trading center on the Niger River, without mentioning Islam at all. This silence suggests that Islam was not yet prominent among its people at that time.

Nri's religious authority spread not through conquest but through priests and titled agents who traveled between Igbo communities to cleanse offenses against the earth deity and consecrate political and social arrangements. This made Nri's influence a moral and ritual network linking otherwise independent towns.

The scholar Onwuejeogwu combined oral king lists and lineage genealogies to propose that the Nri dynasty began near the end of the tenth century, assigning long reigns to early rulers such as Ìfikuánim. These dates, though often treated as exact years, are a modern reconstruction rather than a continuous written record.

culture.text: Islam reached West Africa through traders in the 8th century. Its rules on livelihood, values, dress and practices had such a profound effect that tribalism is less observed among Islamized groups like the Wolof, Hausa, Fula, Songhai, Zarma and Soninke than among non-Islamized groups.

West African music can be split into two broad kinds: Islamic music and indigenous secular music. Islam's influence dates back to at least the 9th century, helped by camels being introduced to trade routes between North Africa and West Africa. Islamic-influenced music often uses stringed instruments like the goje, while secular music leans on drums such as the djembe.

Griots, known as wandering musicians, have traditionally spread music across West Africa. Their purpose is to pass on oral tradition through musical storytelling, and they remain important in preserving the cultures of smaller ethnolinguistic groups.

Arab writers described the Ghana Empire in the 8th century as a wealthy state. Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Fazari called it the "Land of Gold" and said it was equal in size to the Idrisid state of Morocco. It also appeared on Al-Khwarizmi's world map in 833.

Gao was one of the earliest sites of significant trans-Saharan trade, in the 8th century, much earlier than scholars once believed. Its most important trade items were gold, copper, slaves and salt. Compared with Kanem and Wagadu, Gao was not a major center of the slave trade, although slavery was widely practiced within Gao itself. It was also a major manufacturing center, where craftspeople fashioned carnelian into beads that were greatly valued in the Sudan and the West African rainforest.

Before the 10th century, the Do people, talented farmers who raised crops on fertile lands bordering the Niger, were subjugated by more powerful, horse-riding Songhai speakers, who established control over the area. The groups gradually came to speak the same language, and they and their country eventually became known as the Songhai.

Wagadou's slave raids made the Mandekalu a major source of slaves for the empire. One possible response to this pressure was the formation of hunters associations, which doubled as defense associations. These were later federated under a "master of the bush" called the Simbo, who held both military and religious power, and whose power and prestige allowed such individuals to become petty kings.
culture.source_title: Military history of the Mali Empire

culture.text: Archaeologists found two settlements on the eastern bank of the Niger near Gao: Old Gao and Gao-Saney. Imported pottery and glass from Gao-Saney suggest it was occupied between the 8th and 12th centuries. Gao Ancien was the political center and contains the oldest royal palace discovered in the region.

Michael Gomez notes that the term Bilad al-Sudan, literally "land of the Blacks", appeared in Arabic sources from no later than the ninth century and was associated with exporting slaves to the Arab world. Early evidence ties this human trafficking to the Kanem-Bornu Empire around Lake Chad rather than to the Gao or Ghana empires. Gomez contends that trans-Saharan trade went along with associating the Sūdān ever more closely with slaves, calling the idea of Bilad al-Sudan a "racialization of space".
